content.prompt: Sketch $y=x^2+4x-12$

spec.sourceRegion: Guided Practice panel, right-hand reference graph

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}y&=x^2+4x-12\\y&=(x+6)(x-2)\end{align*}$$
$a=1>0$, so the parabola is concave up.

Let $x=0$.
$$\begin{align*}y&=0^2+4(0)-12\\y&=-12\end{align*}$$
The $y$-intercept is $(0,-12)$.

Let $y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}0&=(x+6)(x-2)\\x+6&=0\quad\text{or}\quad x-2=0\\x&=-6\quad\text{or}\quad x=2\end{align*}$$
The $x$-intercepts are $(-6,0)$ and $(2,0)$.

Mean of the $x$-intercepts:
$$\begin{align*}x&=\frac{-6+2}{2}\\x&=-2\end{align*}$$
Substitute $x=-2$:
$$\begin{align*}y&=(-2)^2+4(-2)-12\\y&=-16\end{align*}$$
The turning point is $(-2,-16)$. Sketch a concave-up parabola through the intercepts with this turning point.

answer.worked: $a=2>0$, so the parabola is concave up.

Let $x=0$.
$$\begin{align*}y&=2(0)^2+7(0)+5\\y&=5\end{align*}$$
The $y$-intercept is $(0,5)$.

Let $y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}0&=(2x+5)(x+1)\\2x+5&=0\quad\text{or}\quad x+1=0\\x&=-\frac52\quad\text{or}\quad x=-1\end{align*}$$
The $x$-intercepts are $\left(-\frac52,0\right)$ and $(-1,0)$.

Mean of the $x$-intercepts:
$$x=\frac{-\frac52+(-1)}{2}=-\frac74.$$
Substitute $x=-\frac74$.
$$\begin{align*}y&=2\left(-\frac74\right)^2+7\left(-\frac74\right)+5\\y&=\frac{49}{8}-\frac{49}{4}+5\\y&=-\frac98\end{align*}$$
The vertex is $\left(-\frac74,-\frac98\right)$.

content.prompt: Substitute $y = 0$ then use the null factor law to find the $x$-intercepts of these quadratics.

answer.worked:
At the $x$-intercepts, $y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}0&=(x+1)(x-2)\\x+1&=0\quad\text{or}\quad x-2=0\\x&=-1\quad\text{or}\quad x=2\end{align*}$$

At the $x$-intercepts, $y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}0&=(x-3)(x-4)\\x-3&=0\quad\text{or}\quad x-4=0\\x&=3\quad\text{or}\quad x=4\end{align*}$$

At the $x$-intercepts, $y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}0&=(x+1)(x+5)\\x+1&=0\quad\text{or}\quad x+5=0\\x&=-1\quad\text{or}\quad x=-5\end{align*}$$

At the $x$-intercepts, $y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}0&=x(x-3)\\x&=0\quad\text{or}\quad x-3=0\\x&=0\quad\text{or}\quad x=3\end{align*}$$

At the $x$-intercepts, $y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}0&=2x(x-5)\\2x&=0\quad\text{or}\quad x-5=0\\x&=0\quad\text{or}\quad x=5\end{align*}$$

At the $x$-intercepts, $y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}0&=-3x(x+2)\\-3x&=0\quad\text{or}\quad x+2=0\\x&=0\quad\text{or}\quad x=-2\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Factorise and use the null factor law to find the $x$-intercepts for these quadratics.

answer.worked:
At the $x$-intercepts, $y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}0&=x^2+3x+2\\0&=(x+2)(x+1)\\x+2&=0\quad\text{or}\quad x+1=0\\x&=-2\quad\text{or}\quad x=-1\end{align*}$$

At the $x$-intercepts, $y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}0&=x^2+2x-8\\0&=(x+4)(x-2)\\x+4&=0\quad\text{or}\quad x-2=0\\x&=-4\quad\text{or}\quad x=2\end{align*}$$

At the $x$-intercept, $y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}0&=x^2-8x+16\\0&=(x-4)^2\\x-4&=0\\x&=4\end{align*}$$

At the $x$-intercepts, $y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}0&=x^2-4x\\0&=x(x-4)\\x&=0\quad\text{or}\quad x-4=0\\x&=0\quad\text{or}\quad x=4\end{align*}$$

At the $x$-intercepts, $y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}0&=x^2-6x\\0&=x(x-6)\\x&=0\quad\text{or}\quad x-6=0\\x&=0\quad\text{or}\quad x=6\end{align*}$$

At the $x$-intercepts, $y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}0&=2x^2+10x\\0&=2x(x+5)\\2x&=0\quad\text{or}\quad x+5=0\\x&=0\quad\text{or}\quad x=-5\end{align*}$$

At the $x$-intercepts, $y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}0&=x^2-9\\0&=(x+3)(x-3)\\x+3&=0\quad\text{or}\quad x-3=0\\x&=-3\quad\text{or}\quad x=3\end{align*}$$

At the $x$-intercepts, $y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}0&=x^2-25\\0&=(x+5)(x-5)\\x+5&=0\quad\text{or}\quad x-5=0\\x&=-5\quad\text{or}\quad x=5\end{align*}$$

answer.worked: $a=1>0$, so the parabola is concave up.

Let $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=(0+1)^2\\y&=1\end{aligned}$$
The $y$-intercept is $(0,1)$.

answer.short: $y=(x+2)^2$. Concave up; $y$-intercept $(0,4)$; $x$-intercept and vertex $(-2,0)$; axis of symmetry $x=-2$.
answer.worked:
Factorise:
$$\begin{align*}y&=x^2+4x+4\\y&=(x+2)^2\end{align*}$$
Since $a=1>0$, the parabola is concave up.

For the $y$-intercept, let $x=0$:
$$\begin{align*}y&=0^2+4(0)+4\\y&=4\end{align*}$$
For the $x$-intercept, let $y=0$:
$$\begin{align*}0&=(x+2)^2\\x&=-2\end{align*}$$
The repeated root gives the turning-point coordinate:
$$\begin{align*}x&=\frac{-2+(-2)}{2}\\x&=-2\\y&=(-2)^2+4(-2)+4\\y&=0\end{align*}$$
The vertex is $(-2,0)$ and the axis of symmetry is $x=-2$. The curve touches the $x$-axis at the vertex and passes through $(0,4)$.

answer.worked:
Factorise:
$$\begin{align*}y&=3(x^2+6x+8)\\y&=3(x+4)(x+2)\end{align*}$$
Since $3>0$, the parabola is concave up.
At $x=0$, $y=24$, so the $y$-intercept is $(0,24)$.
For the $x$-intercepts:
$$\begin{align*}0&=3(x+4)(x+2)\\x&=-4\text{ or }-2\end{align*}$$
The vertex lies halfway between the $x$-intercepts:
$$\begin{align*}x&=\frac{-4+(-2)}2\\x&=-3\\y&=3(-3)^2+18(-3)+24\\y&=-3\end{align*}$$
Vertex: $(-3,-3)$.

answer.worked:
Factorise as a difference of squares:
$$y=(3-4x)(3+4x)$$
Since $-16<0$, the parabola is concave down.
At $x=0$, $y=9$, so the $y$-intercept is $(0,9)$.

content.prompt: Sketch $y=(3-x)(2x+4)$, showing the intercepts and the vertex.

answer.worked:
The $x^2$ coefficient is $(-1)(2)=-2<0$, so the parabola is concave down.
Let $x=0$.
$$\begin{align*}y&=(3-0)(0+4)\\y&=12\end{align*}$$
Let $y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}0&=(3-x)(2x+4)\\x&=3\quad\text{or}\quad x=-2\end{align*}$$
Use the mean of the $x$-intercepts.
$$\begin{align*}x&=\frac{-2+3}{2}\\x&=0.5\end{align*}$$
Substitute $x=0.5$.
$$\begin{align*}y&=(3-0.5)(2(0.5)+4)\\y&=12.5\end{align*}$$
The vertex is $(0.5,12.5)$.

answer.worked:
$y=3(x-4)^2-2$

Comparing with $y=a(x-h)^2+k$ gives $h=4$ and $k=-2$. The turning point is $(4,-2)$.

$y=-3(x-4)^2-2$

$h=4$ and $k=-2$, so the turning point is $(4,-2)$. The negative coefficient changes concavity, not the turning point.

$y=\frac{1}{3}(x+4)^2+2$

$h=-4$ and $k=2$, so the turning point is $(-4,2)$. The coefficient $\frac13$ changes width.

$y=\frac{(x+4)^2}{3}+2$

$y=\frac13(x+4)^2+2$, so $h=-4$ and $k=2$. The turning point is $(-4,2)$.

$y=\frac{(x+4)^2+2}{3}$

$y=\frac13(x+4)^2+\frac23$, so $h=-4$ and $k=\frac23$. The turning point is $\left(-4,\frac23\right)$.

$y=(x+4)^2+2$

content.prompt: Write the equation for these parabolas, when compared to $y=x^2$.

answer.worked: Reflection across the $x$-axis changes the sign of the squared term: $y=-x^2$.
A shift left 2 units replaces $x$ with $x+2$: $y=(x+2)^2$.
A shift down 5 units subtracts 5 from the output: $y=x^2-5$.
A shift up 4 units adds 4 to the output: $y=x^2+4$.
A shift right 1 unit replaces $x$ with $x-1$: $y=(x-1)^2$.

Reflection gives a negative coefficient; shifting left 3 units replaces $x$ with $x+3$. Thus $y=-(x+3)^2$.

content.prompt: Sketch $y=(x+3)^2-1$

answer.worked: $a=1>0$, so the parabola is concave up.

Let $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}y&=(0+3)^2-1\\y&=8\end{aligned}$$
The $y$-intercept is $(0,8)$.

Let $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}0&=(x+3)^2-1\\1&=(x+3)^2\\\pm1&=x+3\\-3\pm1&=x\\x&=-4\text{ or }-2\end{aligned}$$
The $x$-intercepts are $(-4,0)$ and $(-2,0)$.
In $y=a(x-h)^2+k$, $h=-3$ and $k=-1$. The vertex is $(-3,-1)$.

answer.short: Upward-opening parabola with vertex $(-3,-1)$, $x$-intercepts $(-4,0)$ and $(-2,0)$, and $y$-intercept $(0,8)$.
answer.worked: Plot the vertex and intercepts. Draw a smooth upward-opening parabola symmetric about $x=-3$.

content.prompt: Sketch each parabola from vertex form.

answer.worked: $a=-1<0$, so the parabola is concave down.

Let $x=0$.
$$\begin{align*}y&=-(0+1)^2+4\\y&=3\end{align*}$$
The $y$-intercept is $(0,3)$.

Let $y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}0&=-(x+1)^2+4\\(x+1)^2&=4\\x+1&=\pm2\\x&=-1\pm2\\x&=-3\text{ or }1\end{align*}$$

children.prompt: State the condition on $a$ and $k$ for $y=a(x-h)^2+k$ to have two $x$-intercepts.

answer.worked:
The vertex is $(h,k)$ and the parabola opens up if $a>0$ and down if $a<0$.

If $a$ and $k$ have opposite signs, the vertex is on the opposite side of the $x$-axis from the way the parabola opens, so it crosses the axis twice.

If $a$ and $k$ have the same sign, the parabola opens away from the axis, so there are no $x$-intercepts.

classification.difficultyReason: Parts a-d require two linked judgements without calculation: the sign of a gives the direction the parabola opens, and the sign of k gives which side of the x-axis the vertex is on. The student then combines these to decide whether the parabola reaches the axis. That is more than reading off a turning point (p17-q5), but each case is routine. Part e is the hardest demand. The student must generalise these case judgements into a symbolic rule ('a and k have opposite signs'), which is a small step of abstraction and reframing. It needs no algebraic solving, no sketching and no multi-step computation. That puts it just below p24-q3, which needs several computed features and a sketch.

Below is the graph of $y = a(x+h)^2$, where $a$ and $h$ are constants.
Which statement is correct?



A. $a > 0, h > 0$
B. $a > 0, h < 0$
C. $a < 0, h > 0$
D. $a < 0, h < 0$

answer.worked:
The parabola opens downwards, so $a<0$. The vertex of $y=a(x+h)^2$ is $(-h,0)$. Since the vertex is to the right of the $y$-axis, $-h>0$, so $h<0$.
Correct answer: D.

content.prompt:
Consider the parabola $y=x^2-8x+4$.
Find the coordinates of the vertex.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}
y &= x^2 - 8x + 4 \\
y &= (x^2 - 8x + 16) - 16 + 4 \\
y &= (x - 4)^2 - 12
\end{align*}$$
The coordinates of the vertex are $(4, -12)$.

\end{align*}$$
The $x$-intercepts are $(4 - \sqrt{6}, 0)$ and $(4 + \sqrt{6}, 0)$.

content.prompt:
What is the minimum value of the function $f(x) = 2x^2 - 4x + 1$?

(A) $-2$
(B) $-1$
(C) $1$
(D) $2$

answer.worked:
Take out the common factor and complete the square.
$$\begin{align*}f(x)&=2(x^2-2x)+1\\f(x)&=2(x^2-2x+1-1)+1\\f(x)&=2((x-1)^2-1)+1\\f(x)&=2(x-1)^2-1\end{align*}$$
The parabola is concave up with vertex $(1,-1)$, so the minimum value is $-1$. The answer is (B).

content.prompt: Consider the quadratic equation $y = 2x^2 - 2x - 4$.

answer.worked:
At the $x$-intercepts, $y=0$.
$$\begin{align*}2x^2-2x-4&=0\\x^2-x-2&=0\\(x-2)(x+1)&=0\\x&=2\quad\text{or}\quad x=-1\end{align*}$$
The $x$-intercepts are $(-1,0)$ and $(2,0)$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Determine the co-ordinates of the vertex.

answer.worked:
The axis of symmetry lies halfway between the $x$-intercepts.
$$\begin{align*}x&=\frac{-1+2}{2}\\x&=\frac{1}{2}\end{align*}$$
Substitute $x=\frac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{align*}y&=2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2-2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)-4\\y&=\frac{1}{2}-1-4\\y&=-\frac{9}{2}\end{align*}$$
The vertex is $\left(\frac{1}{2},-\frac{9}{2}\right)$.

children.prompt:

answer.worked:
Since $a=2>0$, the parabola is concave up.
Let $x=0$: $y=-4$, so the $y$-intercept is $(0,-4)$.
The $x$-intercepts are $(-1,0)$ and $(2,0)$ and the vertex is $\left(\frac{1}{2},-\frac{9}{2}\right)$.
Plot these points and join them with a smooth parabola.

content.prompt:
Given $f(x)$ is a quadratic function with a vertex at $(3,-4)$, which of the following must be true?

(A) $f(x)=0$ has one or more integer roots.
(B) $f(x)-3=0$ has one or more rational roots.
(C) $f(x)+4=0$ has one or more real roots.
(D) $f(x)+5=0$ has no real roots.

answer.worked:
In vertex form, $f(x)=a(x-3)^2-4$ with $a\neq0$.
For $f(x)+4=0$:
$$\begin{align*}a(x-3)^2-4+4&=0\\a(x-3)^2&=0\\x&=3\end{align*}$$
So $f(x)+4=0$ always has the real root $x=3$. The other options depend on the value of $a$. The answer is (C).

The triangle has base $8-2=6$ and perpendicular height $|-9k|=9|k|$. Hence
$$\begin{align*}\text{Area}&=\frac12\times\text{base}\times\text{height}\\\text{Area}&=\frac12(6)(9|k|)\\\text{Area}&=27|k|\text{ square units}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Write the equation in vertex form.

answer.worked:
Complete the square around the midpoint of the two factors:
$$\begin{align*}y&=((x-p-2)+2)((x-p-2)-2)+p\\y&=(x-p-2)^2-4+p\\y&=(x-p-2)^2+p-4.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: State the vertex and axis of symmetry in terms of $p$.

answer.worked: From $y=(x-(p+2))^2+p-4$, the vertex is $(p+2,p-4)$ and the axis of symmetry is $x=p+2$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: As $p$ varies, the vertices lie on a straight line. Find its equation.

answer.worked:
Let the vertex be $(X,Y)$. Since $X=p+2$ and $Y=p-4$,
$$\begin{align*}p&=X-2\\Y&=(X-2)-4\\Y&=X-6.\end{align*}$$
The vertex locus is $y=x-6$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Determine the values of $p$ for which the parabola has:

answer.worked:
For an $x$-intercept,
$$\begin{align*}0&=(x-p-2)^2+p-4\\(x-p-2)^2&=4-p.\end{align*}$$
There are two distinct solutions when $4-p>0$, so $p<4$.
There is exactly one solution to $(x-p-2)^2=4-p$ when $4-p=0$, so $p=4$.
A real square cannot be negative. Thus $(x-p-2)^2=4-p$ has no real solutions when $4-p<0$, so $p>4$.

children.label: e
children.prompt: Find the value of $p$ for which the vertex lies on the $y$-axis.

answer.worked:
The vertex lies on the $y$-axis when its $x$-coordinate is zero:
$$\begin{align*}p+2&=0\\p&=-2.\end{align*}$$
The vertex is then $(0,-6)$.

children.label: f
children.prompt: When the intercepts exist, express them exactly in terms of $p$.

answer.worked:
When $p\leq4$,
$$\begin{align*}(x-p-2)^2&=4-p\\x-p-2&=\pm\sqrt{4-p}\\x&=p+2\pm\sqrt{4-p}.\end{align*}$$
The intercepts are $(p+2-\sqrt{4-p},0)$ and $(p+2+\sqrt{4-p},0)$; they coincide when $p=4$.

flags.note:
[Pedagogy audit v2 · Applied automatically · New teaching] The lesson teaches only monic completing the square, but Q2 and Q3 need taking out the leading coefficient first, then completing the square inside the brackets. A worked example of that method should come before Q2.
Worked example: Sketch $y=2x^2+8x+6$
$$\begin{align*}y&=2(x^2+4x+3)\\y&=2(x^2+4x+4-4+3)\\y&=2((x+2)^2-1)\\y&=2(x+2)^2-2\end{align*}$$
Concavity: $a=2>0$, concave up.

$y$-int: let $x=0$
$$y=2(0+2)^2-2=6$$
$x$-int: let $y=0$
$$\begin{align*}0&=2(x+2)^2-2\\2&=2(x+2)^2&&\color{#ef6068}{+2}\\1&=(x+2)^2&&\color{#ef6068}{\div2}\\x+2&=\pm1\\x&=-3\text{ or }-1\end{align*}$$
Vertex: $(-2,-2)$
Guided practice:
Proposed question: Sketch these parabolas by taking out a common factor, then CTS. Show vertex and intercepts.
a) $y=2x^2-4x-6$
b) $y=3x^2+12x+18$
c) $y=2x^2-16x+20$
Answers: a) $y=2(x-1)^2-8$; concave up. Vertex $(1,-8)$; $x$-intercepts $(-1,0)$ and $(3,0)$; $y$-intercept $(0,-6)$.; b) $y=3(x+2)^2+6$; concave up. Vertex $(-2,6)$; no $x$-intercepts; $y$-intercept $(0,18)$.; c) $y=2(x-4)^2-12$; concave up. Vertex $(4,-12)$; $x$-intercepts $(4-\sqrt6,0)$ and $(4+\sqrt6,0)$; $y$-intercept $(0,20)$.
Applied: Worked example and guided practice added after p29-guided-practice.

MA5-NLI-P-01 interprets and compares non-linear relationships and their transformations, both algebraically and graphically
Graph parabolas and describe their features and transformations
• Use graphing applications to compare parabolas of the form y = kx², y = kx² + c, y = k(x − b)² and y = k(x − b)² + c, and describe their features and transformations

• Determine the equation of the axis of symmetry of a parabola using either the formula x = −b/(2a) or the midpoint of the x-intercepts
• Find the coordinates of a parabola’s vertex using a variety of methods
• Graph quadratic relationships of the form y = ax² + bx + c by identifying and applying features of parabolas and their equations without graphing software

entries.description: Sketching Parabolas from Vertex Form

Sketch Parabolas from Vertex Form
To sketch y = a(x − h)² + k:
1. Determine the concavity.
a > 0, concave up ∪; a < 0 concave down ∩.
2. Find the y-intercept. Substitute x = 0.
3. Find the x-intercepts, if any. Substitute y = 0.
4. Determine the vertex. Using (h, k).

0. Vertex form by CTS

   y = (x² − 4x + 4) − 4 − 5
   y = (x − 2)² − 9
1. Concavity: a > 0, concave up.
2. y-int: Let x = 0,
   y = (0 − 2)² − 9 = −5
3. x-int: Let y = 0
   (x − 2)² − 9 = 0
   (x − 2)² = 9
   x − 2 = ±3
   x = 2 ± 3
   x = 5 or −1

entries.description: Sketching Parabolas by the Quadratic Formula

Sketching Parabolas by Quadratic Formula
Instead of completing the square, we can use the quadratic formula to sketch instead.
1. Concavity.
2. y-int.
3. x-ints using x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/(2a).
4. Vertex using x = −b/(2a), then substitute value of x into the equation to find y.

entries.description: y = x² − 4x + 5
entries.sourceLabel: Page 37, left column; no printed question label

expectedAnswer.short: Concave up; y-intercept (0, 5); Δ = −4, so no x-intercepts; vertex (2, 1).
expectedAnswer.worked:
1. a = 1 > 0, so concave up.
2. Let x = 0: y = 5, so the y-intercept is (0, 5).
3. Δ = b² − 4ac = (−4)² − 4(1)(5) = −4. Since Δ < 0, there are no x-intercepts.
4. x = −b/(2a) = −(−4)/(2 × 1) = 2. Substitute: y = 2² − 4(2) + 5 = 1. Vertex (2, 1).
Sketch an upward-opening parabola with vertex (2, 1), passing through (0, 5), entirely above the x-axis.

entries.description: Show that the discriminant of x² − (p + 1)x + p − 1 = 0 is Δ = (p − 1)² + 4.
Hence explain why the parabola will always have two x-intercepts.
The discriminant Δ = (p − 1)² + 4 is always positive, so always 2 solutions and hence 2 x-intercepts.

entries.description: Show that for y = x² + 2mx + m² + n², the graph is always touching or above the x-axis for all real values of m and n.
entries.presentation: Working space beneath prompt.

entries.description:
Visible source working: Δ = 4m² − 4(m² + n²)
= −4m²
Visible source explanation: −4n² cannot be positive, so either Δ = 0; graph touching x-axis, or Δ < 0; graph is always above the x-axis and never touches it (always above since a>0).

entries.description: Show that y = (p − 3)x² + 6x − (p + 3) will always have x-intercepts that are rational numbers, for all integer values of p (except p = 3).
entries.presentation: Working space beneath prompt.

entries.description:
Δ = 36 + 4(p − 3)(p + 3)
= 36 + 4(p² − 9)
= 4p²
Since the discriminant is always a perfect square, roots will always be rational.
At p = 3 the x² term disappears, so the graph is the straight line y = 6x − 6, which has x intercept of 1.

entries.description:
Rewrite the equation as
y = x² + p(x − 1).
The value is independent of p when x − 1 = 0. Thus x = 1 and
y = 1² = 1.
Every member of the family passes through (1,1).

Here a = 1, b = p and c = −p. Therefore
Δ = b² − 4ac = p² + 4p = p(p + 4).
Tangency requires Δ = 0:
p(p + 4) = 0,
p = 0 or p = −4.

If p = 0,
y = x²,
so the tangency point is (0,0).
If p = −4,
y = x² − 4x + 4 = (x − 2)²,
so the tangency point is (2,0).

entries.description:
Passing through the origin means that one x-intercept is 0. Since the two intercepts are 4 units apart, the other intercept is either 4 or −4.

Case 1: roots 0 and 4.
y = ax(x − 4), a ≠ 0.
The vertex lies midway between the roots, so its x-coordinate is 2. Its y-coordinate is
y = a(2)(−2) = −4a.
Because the vertex lies on y = x − 6,
−4a = 2 − 6 = −4.
Thus a = 1, giving
y = x(x − 4).
Its vertex is (2, −4).

Case 2: roots 0 and −4.
y = ax(x + 4), a ≠ 0.
The vertex has x-coordinate −2 and y-coordinate
y = a(−2)(2) = −4a.
The line gives
−4a = −2 − 6 = −8.
Thus a = 2, giving
y = 2x(x + 4).
Its vertex is (−2, −8).

These are the only possibilities because the second root must be exactly 4 or −4, and in each case the vertex condition determines a unique non-zero value of a.
